6.2 Continual pretraining of foundation model for spatial transcriptomics
6.2.1 Data processing
We employed a comprehensive approach to data acquisition and filtering, focusing on the integration of spatial transcriptomics data. This data was primarily sourced from the CELLxGENE Chanzuckerberg Initiative. [2022] platform and supplemented with datasets hosted on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Our selection criteria were specifically tailored to include only samples processed using Visium or Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) technologies and derived from human tissues. The resultant dataset of around 1 million Visium and ST sites from 278 individual studies, enriched with spatial context, offers a unique opportunity to delve into the complexities of cellular landscapes
Contrasting with the data collection strategy outlined in Section 3.2, which focused exclusively on normal (non-disease) conditions, this phase of data processing incorporated tissue samples from both normal and diseased states. The rationale behind this inclusive approach stems from the burgeoning potential and clinical relevance of spatial profiling technologies. These technologies have shown exceptional promise, particularly in oncological studies and other clinical research domains where the spatial context of gene expression provides critical insights into disease progression, tissue architecture, and cellular microenvironments.
Given the nascent yet rapidly evolving nature of spatial omics, including data from both healthy and diseased tissues enables us to capture a broader spectrum of cellular interactions and states. This dual-focus approach is especially pertinent in oncology, where understanding the spatial dynamics of tumor cells in relation to their microenvironment can yield groundbreaking insights into tumor biology, metastasis, and treatment responses. Furthermore, by encompassing a diverse array of conditions, we enhance the robustness and applicability of our models, ensuring they are well-equipped to handle a wide range of spatial transcriptomics data.
In processing this spatial omics data, we adopted quality control measures to ensure the integrity and reliability of the data. This involved filtering out samples with inadequate quality or insufficient metadata, thus maintaining a high standard of data quality.

Adaptation of Input Embeddings for Spatial Omics
In the process of continual pretraining for spatial omics, we have incorporated modifications to the input embedding strategy, as initially described in Section 3.3.1. This includes the integration of two new special tokens, which are specifically designed to address the observed high variability in sequencing depth and the number of genes across different sample slides and even within different regions of the same slide.
Integration of special Tokens To address the specificities of spatial omics data, we introduce two new special tokens: < num of genes > and < total counts > . These tokens are appended right after the < cls > token in the input sequence. The identifiers (ids) for these new tokens are added to the existing vocabulary, expanding the model's linguistic repertoire to better represent spatial transcriptomic data.
The < num of genes > token is designed to capture the count of sequenced genes with non-zero expressions in each individual spatial spot. It is encoded as an integer identifier, similar to the gene tokens. This token provides a quantitative measure of gene activity within a spatial sample, aiding the model in assessing the richness of the gene expression profile. Similarly, the < total counts > token encapsulates the total expression count of these genes before binning. This token offers a summary measure of overall gene expression intensity within a spot.
Rationale for New Tokens The rationale behind introducing these tokens is grounded in our observation of technical variations inherent in spatial omics data. Sequencing depth and gene count variability can significantly impact the model's ability to learn robust and accurate embeddings for spots and genes. By incorporating these new tokens, we provide the model with additional contextual information that aids in normalizing these technical variations, thereby enabling the generation of more consistent and reliable embeddings. The < num of genes > token helps the model account for the richness of the gene expression profile in a given spatial spot, while the < total counts > token provides a summary measure of overall gene expression intensity, crucial for understanding spatial patterns and distributions.
Updated Input Embedding Equation As per the original input embedding approach, each gene is assigned a unique identifier. For spatial transcriptomics, the gene tokens and their corresponding expression values are augmented with these new spatial-specific tokens, enriching the input data representation.
The final input embedding vector for each spatial spot is modified to include the embeddings for the new tokens, along with the existing gene tokens and condition tokens. The equation for the modified input vector is as follows:

In this updated equation, the identifiers for < num of genes > and < total counts > are appended right after the < cls > token, followed by the identifiers of the gene tokens. This structure ensures that the model receives the additional contextual information at the outset of processing each input spot.
The embedding layers are extended to process the new spatial-specific tokens alongside the traditional gene tokens and condition tokens. The final embedding for each spatial spot thus encompasses a comprehensive representation, integrating both the spatial context and the gene-level information.

To collect diverse and extensive sequencing data for the self-supervised pre-training of scGPT, we assembled 33 million scRNA-seq data of human cells under normal (non-disease) conditions, obtained via the CELLxGENE collection [Chanzuckerberg Initiative., 2022]. This comprehensive dataset encompasses a wide range of cell types from 51 organs/tissues and 441 studies, providing a rich representation of cellular heterogeneity across the human body.

#### 3.2.1 Data collection

We collected data for the whole-human foundation model pre-training from the CELLxGENE portal [Chanzuckerberg Initiative., 2022] using the Census API 1 . We included sequencing protocols of scRNA-seq and snRNA-seq and filtered in samples without disease conditions. This resulted in sequencing data of 33 million cells. We also trained several organ-specific models on samples from individual organs and tissues. For example, we retrieved over 10.3 million human blood and bone marrow scRNA-seq samples [Chanzuckerberg Initiative., 2022] for the pre-training of the scGPT blood model specifically. A total of 65 datasets were collected from CELLxGENE by filtering on Organism (i.e., Homo sapiens), Tissue (i.e., blood, bone marrow), and Disease (i.e., normal, COVID-19, influenza). Additionally, we collected 5.7 million cells of various cancer types to train a pan-cancer model.

#### 3.2.2 Data processing

The single-cell sequencing data is processed into a cell-by-gene matrix, X ∈ R N × G , where each element X i,j ∈ R + represents the read count of an RNA molecule in the case of scRNAseq or a peak region in the case of scATAC-seq. Specifically, in scRNA-seq, the element denotes the RNA abundance for gene j ∈ 0 , 1 , . . . , G in cell i ∈ 0 , 1 , . . . , N . In subsequent sections, we will refer to this matrix as the raw matrix. The input to scGPT consists of three main components: (1) gene (or peak) tokens, (2) expression values, and (3) condition tokens. For each modelling task, the gene tokens and expression values are pre-processed from the raw count matrix X accordingly.

A fundamental challenge in gene expression modelling is the variability in absolute magnitudes across different sequencing protocols [Sarkar and Stephens, 2021]. Variations in sequencing depths and the presence of sparsely expressed genes result in significant differences in data scales among different batches of sequencing samples. These differences are not easily mitigated with common preprocessing techniques such as transcripts per million (TPM) normalization and log 1 p transformation [Haque et al., 2017]. Even after these transformations, the same absolute value can convey different 'semantic' meanings across sequencing batches. To address this scale difference, we propose the value binning technique to convert all expression counts into relative values. For each non-zero expression count in each cell, we calculate the raw absolute values and divide them into B consecutive intervals [ b k , b k +1 ], where k ∈ { 1 , 2 , . . . , B } . Each interval represents an equal portion of all expressed genes (1 /B ). The foundation model is designed to be a generalizable feature extractor that can benefit a diverse range of downstream tasks. Self-attention has been widely used to capture the co-occurrence patterns among tokens. data_source_sections.text:
We employed a comprehensive approach to data acquisition and filtering, focusing on the integration of spatial transcriptomics data. This data was primarily sourced from the CELLxGENE Chanzuckerberg Initiative. [2022] platform and supplemented with datasets hosted on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Our selection criteria were specifically tailored to include only samples processed using Visium or Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) technologies and derived from human tissues. The resultant dataset of around 1 million Visium and ST sites from 278 individual studies, enriched with spatial context, offers a unique opportunity to delve into the complexities of cellular landscapes

Contrasting with the data collection strategy outlined in Section 3.2, which focused exclusively on normal (non-disease) conditions, this phase of data processing incorporated tissue samples from both normal and diseased states. The rationale behind this inclusive approach stems from the burgeoning potential and clinical relevance of spatial profiling technologies. These technologies have shown exceptional promise, particularly in oncological studies and other clinical research domains where the spatial context of gene expression provides critical insights into disease progression, tissue architecture, and cellular microenvironments.

Given the nascent yet rapidly evolving nature of spatial omics, including data from both healthy and diseased tissues enables us to capture a broader spectrum of cellular interactions and states. This dual-focus approach is especially pertinent in oncology, where understanding the spatial dynamics of tumor cells in relation to their microenvironment can yield groundbreaking insights into tumor biology, metastasis, and treatment responses. Furthermore, by encompassing a diverse array of conditions, we enhance the robustness and applicability of our models, ensuring they are well-equipped to handle a wide range of spatial transcriptomics data.

In processing this spatial omics data, we adopted quality control measures to ensure the integrity and reliability of the data. This involved filtering out samples with inadequate quality or insufficient metadata, thus maintaining a high standard of data quality.

To collect diverse and extensive sequencing data for the self-supervised pre-training of scGPT, we assembled 33 million scRNA-seq data of human cells under normal (non-disease) conditions, obtained via the CELLxGENE collection [Chanzuckerberg Initiative., 2022]. #### 3.2.1 Data collection

We collected data for the whole-human foundation model pre-training from the CELLxGENE portal [Chanzuckerberg Initiative., 2022] using the Census API 1 . We included sequencing protocols of scRNA-seq and snRNA-seq and filtered in samples without disease conditions. This resulted in sequencing data of 33 million cells. We also trained several organ-specific models on samples from individual organs and tissues. For example, we retrieved over 10.3 million human blood and bone marrow scRNA-seq samples [Chanzuckerberg Initiative., 2022] for the pre-training of the scGPT blood model specifically. A total of 65 datasets were collected from CELLxGENE by filtering on Organism (i.e., Homo sapiens), Tissue (i.e., blood, bone marrow), and Disease (i.e., normal, COVID-19, influenza). The single-cell sequencing data is processed into a cell-by-gene matrix, X ∈ R N × G , where each element X i,j ∈ R + represents the read count of an RNA molecule in the case of scRNAseq or a peak region in the case of scATAC-seq. Specifically, in scRNA-seq, the element denotes the RNA abundance for gene j ∈ 0 , 1 , . . . , G in cell i ∈ 0 , 1 , . . . , N . #### 3.3.4 Generative pre-training

##### Foundation model pre-training

The foundation model is designed to be a generalizable feature extractor that can benefit a diverse range of downstream tasks. The token vocabulary used in pre-training contains the entire set of genes in the human genome. The expression values were binned prior to model pre-training (Section 3.3.1). To speed up the training, we restrict the input to only genes with non-zero expression for each input cell. To efficiently train the model to capture gene-gene relation and gene-cell relation, we introduce a new generative training strategy with specialized attention masks as described in the following section.

##### Attention mask for generative pre-training

Self-attention has been widely used to capture the co-occurrence patterns among tokens. In natural language processing, this has been achieved mainly in two ways: (1) masked token prediction used in transformer encoder models such as BERT [Devlin et al., 2018] and Roberta [Liu et al., 2019a], where randomly masked tokens in the input sequence are predicted in the model's output; (2) auto-regressive generation with sequential prediction in causal transformer decoder models such as the OpenAI GPT series [Radford et al., 2019, Brown et al., 2020, OpenAI et al., 2023]. The generative pre-training used in OpenAI GPT3 [Brown et al., 2020] and GPT4 [OpenAI et al., 2023] employs a unified framework in which the model predicts the most likely next token from a 'prompt' consisting of known input tokens. This framework offers great flexibility to be utilized in various natural language generation (NLG) applications and demonstrates new capabilities such as contextual awareness in zero-shot and fine-tuned settings [Bubeck et al., 2023]. We believe that generative training can be beneficial to single-cell models in a similar manner. Specifically, we are interested in two tasks: (1) generating unknown gene expression values based on known gene expression, i.e., generation by 'gene prompts', and (2) generating whole genome expression given an input cell type condition, i.e., generation by 'cell prompts'.

Despite similar ideas of tokens and prompts, modelling genetic reads is inherently different from natural language due to the non-sequential nature of the data. Unlike words in a sentence, the order of genes within a cell is interchangeable, and there is no equivalent concept of the 'next gene' to predict. This makes it challenging to apply the causal masking formulation from GPT models directly in single-cell data. To address this challenge, we developed a specialized attention masking mechanism for scGPT that defines the order of prediction based on attention scores.

6.2.1 Data processing
We employed a comprehensive approach to data acquisition and filtering, focusing on the integration of spatial transcriptomics data. This data was primarily sourced from the CELLxGENE Chanzuckerberg Initiative. [2022] platform and supplemented with datasets hosted on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Our selection criteria were specifically tailored to include only samples processed using Visium or Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) technologies and derived from human tissues. The resultant dataset of around 1 million Visium and ST sites from 278 individual studies, enriched with spatial context, offers a unique opportunity to delve into the complexities of cellular landscapes
Contrasting with the data collection strategy outlined in Section 3.2, which focused exclusively on normal (non-disease) conditions, this phase of data processing incorporated tissue samples from both normal and diseased states. The rationale behind this inclusive approach stems from the burgeoning potential and clinical relevance of spatial profiling technologies. These technologies have shown exceptional promise, particularly in oncological studies and other clinical research domains where the spatial context of gene expression provides critical insights into disease progression, tissue architecture, and cellular microenvironments.
Given the nascent yet rapidly evolving nature of spatial omics, including data from both healthy and diseased tissues enables us to capture a broader spectrum of cellular interactions and states. This dual-focus approach is especially pertinent in oncology, where understanding the spatial dynamics of tumor cells in relation to their microenvironment can yield groundbreaking insights into tumor biology, metastasis, and treatment responses. Furthermore, by encompassing a diverse array of conditions, we enhance the robustness and applicability of our models, ensuring they are well-equipped to handle a wide range of spatial transcriptomics data.
In processing this spatial omics data, we adopted quality control measures to ensure the integrity and reliability of the data. This involved filtering out samples with inadequate quality or insufficient metadata, thus maintaining a high standard of data quality.

Adaptation of Input Embeddings for Spatial Omics
In the process of continual pretraining for spatial omics, we have incorporated modifications to the input embedding strategy, as initially described in Section 3.3.1. This includes the integration of two new special tokens, which are specifically designed to address the observed high variability in sequencing depth and the number of genes across different sample slides and even within different regions of the same slide.
Integration of special Tokens To address the specificities of spatial omics data, we introduce two new special tokens: < num of genes > and < total counts > . These tokens are appended right after the < cls > token in the input sequence. The identifiers (ids) for these new tokens are added to the existing vocabulary, expanding the model's linguistic repertoire to better represent spatial transcriptomic data.
The < num of genes > token is designed to capture the count of sequenced genes with non-zero expressions in each individual spatial spot. It is encoded as an integer identifier, similar to the gene tokens. This token provides a quantitative measure of gene activity within a spatial sample, aiding the model in assessing the richness of the gene expression profile. Similarly, the < total counts > token encapsulates the total expression count of these genes before binning. This token offers a summary measure of overall gene expression intensity within a spot.
Rationale for New Tokens The rationale behind introducing these tokens is grounded in our observation of technical variations inherent in spatial omics data. Sequencing depth and gene count variability can significantly impact the model's ability to learn robust and accurate embeddings for spots and genes. By incorporating these new tokens, we provide the model with additional contextual information that aids in normalizing these technical variations, thereby enabling the generation of more consistent and reliable embeddings. The < num of genes > token helps the model account for the richness of the gene expression profile in a given spatial spot, while the < total counts > token provides a summary measure of overall gene expression intensity, crucial for understanding spatial patterns and distributions.
Updated Input Embedding Equation As per the original input embedding approach, each gene is assigned a unique identifier. For spatial transcriptomics, the gene tokens and their corresponding expression values are augmented with these new spatial-specific tokens, enriching the input data representation.
The final input embedding vector for each spatial spot is modified to include the embeddings for the new tokens, along with the existing gene tokens and condition tokens. The equation for the modified input vector is as follows:
<!-- formula-not-decoded -->
In this updated equation, the identifiers for < num of genes > and < total counts > are appended right after the < cls > token, followed by the identifiers of the gene tokens. This structure ensures that the model receives the additional contextual information at the outset of processing each input spot.
The embedding layers are extended to process the new spatial-specific tokens alongside the traditional gene tokens and condition tokens. The final embedding for each spatial spot thus encompasses a comprehensive representation, integrating both the spatial context and the gene-level information.
